seo.title: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) vs HagiCode: Features and Comparison
seo.description: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) is DeepSeek's open-source agent harness; HagiCode runs it in a workbench. Compare features, pricing, maturity and fit.

summary: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) is DeepSeek AI's open-source agent harness, still in developer preview, and HagiCode is a workbench that runs dsh as one of its executors. Use dsh alone to try its plugin-based harness or script it; add HagiCode for parallel sessions, proposals and managed commits around it.

content: DeepSeek Harness, command `dsh`, is an open-source agent harness from DeepSeek AI. It runs as a local Web UI, a headless one-shot command, an SDK server or an ACP server, and almost every part of it is a plugin. HagiCode is a desktop and web AI programming workbench that drives agent CLIs, dsh among them, as its executor. It does not replace dsh; HagiCode starts dsh in its ACP mode and adds sessions, proposals and commit handling around it.

dsh is a developer preview whose own safety notice says it is experimental, unaudited and subject to breaking changes. If you want to explore the harness itself, write plugins or script it, stay with dsh alone. If you want to run it next to other agents with proposals and parallel sessions, HagiCode is the layer for that.

sections.title: DeepSeek Harness vs HagiCode at a glance

cells: What it is
Open-source agent harness from DeepSeek AI, built from plugins on the Cordis framework; developer preview
Workbench that runs agent CLIs, dsh included, as executors
Interface and platforms
Local Web UI (`dsh web`), headless, SDK over stdio JSON-RPC, ACP; needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+
Desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux), Docker Compose container, Microsoft Store edition
Pricing and licensing
MIT-licensed and free to run; you pay your model provider
Desktop and Container free; Store edition free with optional one-time TurboEngine purchase
Model and provider access
DeepSeek API key, catalog providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Moonshot, Z.ai and more), custom OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible endpoints
Hosts no models; sends provider and model to dsh; optional OmniRoute routing
Parallel work
Sessions in the Web UI; the agent can delegate work inside a session
Several sessions at once, each a named Agent with visible status
Spec and planning workflow
The agent maintains a plan inside a session; no proposal lifecycle
OpenSpec proposals: propose, validate, apply, archive (3 concurrent free, 32 with TurboEngine)
Git and commit handling
Runs shell commands in the workspace; its docs include a GitHub review guide
AI-composed commit messages with the repository locked during the commit; Git and GitHub integration
Setup effort
`npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web`, then add a model key under Settings, Models
Desktop install, plus dsh on PATH and a configured model
Best for
Developers who want an open, hackable harness and accept preview software
People running dsh next to other agents, with traceable specs

items.title: Everything is a plugin
content: dsh treats the model adapter, agent loop and interface as plugins composed through Cordis. Each profile has its own plugin set and a `cordis.patch.yml` for overrides, and `dsh plugin --profile <name> add <package>` installs a plugin into a profile. If you want to change how an agent harness behaves, that is the point of the project.

items.title: Four run modes from one binary
content: `dsh web` serves the browser UI. `dsh headless "run the tests"` answers one task and exits, reads a task from stdin, can emit newline-delimited JSON events and can resume a session by id. The sdk profile serves JSON-RPC over stdio, with a Python SDK guide, and the acp profile serves editors and automation clients.

items.title: Model flexibility without a rebuild
content: In Settings, Models you enter a DeepSeek API key, pick a catalog provider, or define a custom endpoint speaking OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses or Anthropic Messages. Model changes apply on the next request, and keys are write-only after saving, stored in `$DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml`.

items.title: Open about its maturity
content: The README warns of compatibility-breaking changes, SAFETY.md calls the software experimental and not production-ready, and releases are alpha tags. The repository was created in August 2026, so expect fast change; that candor is useful when you decide where to run it.

sections.title: When to choose DeepSeek Harness, and when to choose HagiCode

items: you want to try DeepSeek's own harness, or build and test dsh plugins;
you want a local Web UI over an agent without installing another app;
you script one-shot tasks with `dsh headless` or build on the SDK or ACP profiles;
you are comfortable with preview software and breaking changes between releases;
you only ever use DeepSeek models or one gateway.
you want to run dsh next to Claude Code, Codex or other agent CLIs in one workspace;
you want several dsh sessions at once, each tracked as a named Agent;
you want each change to start as an OpenSpec proposal with validation and archive;
you want AI-composed commit messages and an embedded Code Server editor;
you want what dsh learns saved to a Vault, and multi-repository changes described once in Monospecs.

blocks.title: Where HagiCode is not the right tool for dsh users
content: Scripted or CI runs: call `dsh headless` or the SDK directly; HagiCode is a desktop and web app.
dsh already ships a Web UI, so if all you want is a browser front end for dsh, HagiCode is more than you need.
It needs dsh installed and a model configured first, and HagiCode checks that `dsh --help` identifies DeepSeek Harness, so look-alike binaries are refused.
dsh is a preview: a breaking release can break the ACP integration until both sides catch up.
Free editions cap concurrent proposals at 3, and teams that do not want spec discipline will find proposals overhead.
HagiCode is not an IDE replacement for deep manual editing beyond the embedded Code Server.

sections.title: Using DeepSeek Harness together with HagiCode

content: HagiCode runs dsh as a subprocess in its ACP profile, in the repository you open, and passes the provider and model you choose. HagiCode exposes no credential fields for dsh, so sign-in and model keys stay in dsh.
Nothing is locked in: dsh remains a normal install that you can run with `dsh web` or `dsh headless` at any time.

items: Install Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, then `npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh`, so a `dsh` command is on your PATH.
Configure at least one model provider in dsh, for example a DeepSeek API key in its Web UI under Settings, Models.
Install HagiCode Desktop (Windows, macOS or Linux; free) and choose DeepSeek Harness as the Agent CLI.
Set the provider and model together, with the model id exactly as dsh lists it; HagiCode forwards it unsplit.
Open a repository and start a session or proposal. HagiCode always boots `dsh --profile acp` and rejects a `--profile` in extra arguments; the startup timeout defaults to 45 seconds.
To go back to plain dsh, run it directly in the same directory.

blocks.title: What works for dsh inside HagiCode
content: Parallel sessions, Agents management, OpenSpec proposals, AI commit, Code Server, Monospecs, Vault and the unified tool-call view apply to dsh sessions. dsh accepts a provider id such as `omniroute`, so OmniRoute can sit underneath if you set it up as a dsh provider.
Interactive questions are limited to Claude, Pi, OMP and Reasonix, and the agent work panel is Claude only, so neither is available with dsh.

sections.title: What HagiCode adds on top of any agent

items.title: Parallel sessions and Agents management
content: Run several dsh sessions at once, each with its own context, and see which is running, waiting or done. dsh's own sub-agent delegation stays inside a session; HagiCode adds the layer above.

items.title: OpenSpec proposals
content: Start each task as a proposal, discuss the approach with dsh inside it, then let dsh implement within that scope. Because dsh is a preview, the written proposal also records what you changed when a later release behaves differently.

items.title: AI commit and Code Server
content: HagiCode writes the commit message from the diff and locks the repository during the commit, so dsh output ends up as a clean history. Code Server opens the files dsh touched in a browser editor.

items.title: Monospecs and Vault
content: Monospecs lists your sub-repositories in `.hagicode/monospecs.yaml`, so a cross-repo change reaches dsh as one proposal. Vault stores reference projects and notes you register once and reuse.

items.title: OmniRoute, tool-call view and usage
content: OmniRoute centralises model routing across agents. dsh tool calls show in the same typed view as every other agent's, and optional TokenMonitor puts today's tokens and cost in the status bar.

items: dsh is an open-source, plugin-based harness from DeepSeek AI, still in developer preview.
HagiCode does not compete with it: it runs dsh and adds parallel Agents, proposals, commits and a knowledge base, at the cost of an extra install.
Use dsh alone to explore, script or build plugins; use HagiCode plus dsh when it is one of several agents in real project work.

faq.question: Is DeepSeek Harness (dsh) free?
faq.answer: dsh is MIT-licensed and free to run. You pay your model provider, for example through a DeepSeek API key; see the provider's pricing page for rates.

faq.question: How do I install dsh?
faq.answer: The official README runs it with `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web`, which starts a Web UI at http://127.0.0.1:3080, and needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+. For HagiCode, install it globally with `npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh` so `dsh` is on your PATH.

faq.question: Is dsh ready for production?
faq.answer: No, by its own statement. The README says dsh is a developer preview with compatibility-breaking changes, and SAFETY.md says it is experimental, unaudited and not production-ready.

faq.question: Can I use dsh with HagiCode?
faq.answer: Yes. HagiCode starts dsh in its ACP profile, passes the provider and model you choose, and checks that `dsh --help` identifies DeepSeek Harness. Install dsh and configure a model first.

faq.question: Does HagiCode replace dsh?
faq.answer: No. dsh is the executor; HagiCode is the workbench around it, and you can still run dsh directly.

faq.question: dsh vs HagiCode: which should I pick?
faq.answer: Pick dsh alone to explore the harness, write plugins or script one-shot tasks. Add HagiCode when dsh is one of several agents and you want parallel sessions, proposals and managed commits.
